title: Kantian ethics
subtitle: Summary of lecture 4 and Groundwork II
subject: Philosophy: ethics

sources.title: Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals (1785), tr. T. K. Abbott (1895)

blocks.title: The question
blocks.body:
Kant asks what makes an action *morally* good. His answer: not its consequences and not the inclinations behind it, but the **will** that acts from duty, that is, out of respect for a law reason gives itself.

The supreme principle of that law is the **categorical imperative**.
The only thing good without qualification: a will that acts from duty, whatever it achieves.
The subjective principle of an action: *in situation S I will do A to achieve E*.

blocks.title: Hypothetical and categorical imperatives
blocks.body: A **hypothetical** imperative commands an action as a means to something one wants ("If you want X, do Y"). A **categorical** imperative commands unconditionally, for every rational being.

blocks.quote: Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law.

blocks.title: Applying the FUL
points: State the maxim with the agent's real reasons.
Imagine it as a universal law of nature.
Can the world with that law be **conceived**? If not: violation of a perfect duty.
Could a rational agent **will** that world? If not: violation of an imperfect duty.

blocks.title: The Formula of Humanity
blocks.body:
"So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person or in that of any other, in every case as an end withal, never as means only." (4:429)

Using someone as a means is fine (the baker sells you bread); using them **merely** as a means, in a way they could not consent to, is not.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.body: The FUL is **not** a consequence test ("what if everyone did it? That would be bad"). The problem is a *contradiction*: the universalised maxim undermines itself or cannot be rationally willed. Writing the consequentialist version in an exam loses most of the marks.

blocks.title: Objections
blocks.body:
- **Rigorism**: the murderer at the door. Kant (1797) holds that lying is wrong even then; many Kantians instead refine the maxim or appeal to the Formula of Humanity.
- **Empty formalism** (Hegel): the test seems to accept or reject maxims depending on how they are described.
- **Conflicts of duty**: the theory gives little guidance when duties clash.

blocks.title: Exam-style question
blocks.body: Does the Formula of Universal Law forbid lying to the murderer at the door? Discuss.
blocks.solution: Outline: (1) reconstruct the maxim and the FUL test; (2) Kant's own answer in *On a Supposed Right to Lie*; (3) the redescription strategy and its risk of formalism; (4) Korsgaard-style reply via the Formula of Humanity or a two-level reading; (5) your verdict with a reason.
